pedagogy.summary: Moon phases are the single most misconceived topic in school astronomy. The child must build a working Sun-Earth-Moon geometric model in which the Moon is always half-lit by the Sun, and a phase is simply how much of that lit half we happen to see from Earth as the Moon orbits over ~29.5 days. The decisive move is to separate two things children conflate: phases (an every-month consequence of viewing geometry) and eclipses (rare alignments where one body's shadow falls on another). Teach phases first, purely as 'which fraction of the sunlit side faces us', then treat solar (Moon between Sun and Earth) and lunar (Earth between Sun and Moon) eclipses as the special cases when the three bodies line up. Kinaesthetic modelling — each child holding a ball ('Moon') at arm's length and turning while a lamp acts as the Sun — is the best-evidenced route because it puts the child at Earth's viewpoint and lets them literally see a crescent become gibbous become full as they rotate.
bestPractices: Run the ball-and-lamp (or head-as-Earth) kinaesthetic model where each child holds a polystyrene ball at arm's length and slowly turns: they watch the lit fraction facing them grow and shrink, experiencing the full phase cycle from the Earth-centred viewpoint

Insist on the two-viewpoint discipline: show the God's-eye view (Moon orbiting a lit Earth, always half-illuminated) AND the Earth-based view (what a person actually sees in the sky) side by side, and repeatedly translate between them

Teach phases and eclipses as separate ideas in that order; explicitly contrast 'phases happen every month from geometry' with 'eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted, so alignment is uncommon'
Name and sequence the phases with the waxing/waning vocabulary tied to the geometry (waxing = lit part growing as the Moon moves toward the far side of Earth from the Sun)
Directly confront the Earth's-shadow misconception by asking children to locate where Earth's shadow points relative to the Sun, and show that in most phases the Moon is nowhere near it
keyRepresentations: Sun-Earth-Moon orbital diagram showing the Moon always half-lit, with eight positions round the orbit and the matching Earth-view phase drawn beside each
The ball-and-lamp physical model (child's head = Earth, ball = Moon, single bright lamp = Sun)
Phase strip / circular sequence: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent
Eclipse alignment diagram distinguishing umbra/penumbra and the straight-line Sun-Moon-Earth (solar) vs Sun-Earth-Moon (lunar) arrangements
commonMisconceptions: Phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the dominant misconception; actually that is a lunar eclipse, which is rare)
Phases are caused by clouds, or by planets/other bodies blocking the Moon
The Moon is only present in the sky at night, or the far side is permanently dark ('dark side of the Moon')
A solar and a lunar eclipse are the same event, or an eclipse happens every month (fails to account for the Moon's tilted orbit)
The Moon does not rotate / the phase is a fixed property of the Moon rather than of the viewing geometry

learn.summary: Help 11-12 year-olds build a working Sun-Earth-Moon geometric model in which the Moon is always half-lit by the Sun, and a phase is simply how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the Moon orbits over roughly 29.5 days. The decisive teaching move is to separate two ideas learners routinely conflate: phases (an every-month consequence of viewing geometry) and eclipses (rare alignments where one body's shadow falls on another). Teach phases first, purely as 'which fraction of the sunlit side faces us', then treat solar (Moon between Sun and Earth) and lunar (Earth between Sun and Moon) eclipses as the special cases when the three bodies line up. Kinaesthetic modelling, linked orbit/sky views, a labelled phase reference, and sequencing/matching checks each contribute a distinct part of this learning.

activities.title: Ball-and-lamp phase cycle (head as Earth)
feedback: If you predicted 'my head's shadow makes the dark part', that is the common Earth's-shadow misconception. Look at the crescent position: the ball is on the lamp's side of your head, so your head's shadow falls behind you, far from the ball, yet most of the ball facing you is dark. That dark part is the ball's own unlit side. At the full position, raising the ball slightly keeps it just above your head's shadow, so it looks fully lit.
If the ball never looks 'full' as you turn, check you are holding it slightly above head height so your own head doesn't block the lamp each time.
Waxing means the lit part is growing as the Moon moves toward the side of your head away from the lamp; waning means it is shrinking.
activities.rationale: Putting the learner physically at Earth's viewpoint lets them see a crescent become gibbous become full by rotating, directly experiencing phases as viewing geometry. The predict-then-turn structure surfaces the Earth's-shadow misconception so it can be confronted with what is actually observed.

The belief that Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is a widespread and persistent student misconception, distinct from the actual cause (changing Sun-Earth-Moon viewing geometry).
learnerActions: In a darkened room, use a single bright lamp as the Sun and hold a polystyrene ball on a stick at arm's length as the Moon, held slightly above head height, with your own head as the Earth.

Before turning, PREDICT with a reason: as you slowly turn the ball around your head, will it go through crescent → half → full, and what makes the dark part? Commit to your prediction out loud or in writing.
Slowly turn on the spot and watch the lit fraction of the ball facing you grow and shrink through the full cycle.

When the ball looks 'full', deliberately look for where your head's (Earth's) shadow points and check whether it passes just below the raised ball (it should if the lamp is at about head height or higher).
Name each phase as it appears using waxing/waning vocabulary tied to the geometry (waxing = the lit part growing).
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun always lights half the Moon; a phase is how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the viewing angle changes. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not Earth's shadow — and at the 'full' position your head's shadow passes just below the raised ball and misses it entirely, so no shadow is dimming it.

activities.title: Linked orbit view and sky view
feedback: At full Moon, if you expected Earth's shadow to darken the Moon, notice the full Moon still shows its fully lit face. Earth's shadow does extend toward the Moon's side of the sky (opposite the Sun), but the tilted orbit usually carries the Moon just above or below it, so no eclipse happens most months.
If you think an eclipse should happen every month, use the tilt control: in most months the Moon rides slightly high or low of the line-up, so the shadow misses.

A crescent in the sky view corresponds to the Moon being roughly between you and the Sun, so mostly its unlit side faces you — and Earth's shadow, which always points away from the Sun, is then on the far opposite side of the sky, nowhere near the Moon.
activities.rationale: The core idea is a live geometric relationship: as orbital position changes, the visible fraction of the sunlit side changes. Linking a top-down orbit panel to the Earth-based sky panel lets learners watch the phase morph in real time and test the shadow misconception by manipulation. A free-viewpoint 3D version can additionally make the orbital tilt and eclipse rarity vivid by letting the learner tilt the orbital plane and see the shadow miss Earth; it offers a different spatial experience and may add control complexity for this age group.

The belief that Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is a widespread and persistent student misconception, distinct from the actual cause (changing Sun-Earth-Moon viewing geometry).
learnerActions: Work with two linked views side by side: a top-down Sun-Earth-Moon diagram where you move the Moon around its orbit of a fixed, brightly lit Earth, and a synchronized view of how the Moon would appear from Earth.
In the top-down view keep in mind the Moon is always half-lit toward the Sun; move it step by step around the orbit.
At each position, read off the matching Earth-view phase and say why that fraction is visible.
Park the Moon at the 'full' position, then trace where Earth's shadow points relative to the Sun and notice it extends toward the Moon's side of the sky.

Use a 'line up the three bodies' challenge that arranges them in a row to show eclipse geometry, and a tilt control that lifts the Moon's orbit slightly high or low to show how the shadow usually misses.
Keep translating between the two viewpoints: the God's-eye orbit and what a person actually sees in the sky.
activities.intendedInsight: Coupling the orbit view to the sky view shows the phase morph continuously and lets learners test the Earth's-shadow account against what they actually see — it does not fit, most clearly for a crescent. At full Moon the lit face is turned fully toward us; Earth's shadow does point to the Moon's side of the sky (away from the Sun), but the Moon's tilted orbit usually carries it just above or below the shadow, which is why most full Moons are ordinary, not lunar eclipses. For a crescent, by contrast, the Moon is near the Sun's direction so Earth's shadow is on the far opposite side, nowhere near the Moon — the dark part is simply the Moon's own unlit side.

activities.title: Phase-wheel reference and 'why this phase?'
feedback: If you cannot explain 'why this phase', return to the linked orbit/sky view and find the matching orbital position.
Check that you place a solar eclipse with the Moon between Sun and Earth, and a lunar eclipse with Earth between Sun and Moon.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram cannot show the continuous morphing or let the learner manipulate the geometry, but it is a useful reference and consolidation layer for naming the eight phases and recording the umbra/penumbra and alignment facts.

learnerActions: Study a labelled phase sequence: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.
For each phase, lift a flap or reveal the answer to 'why this phase?' and relate the sky appearance to the Moon's orbital position.
Compare the phase wheel to an eclipse alignment diagram that distinguishes umbra and penumbra and the straight-line Sun-Moon-Earth (solar) versus Sun-Earth-Moon (lunar) arrangements.
Use this as a consolidation reference after the hands-on and linked-view work.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming and ordering the phases consolidates the cycle, and placing the phase wheel beside the eclipse diagram keeps the two ideas distinct: monthly phases from viewing angle versus rare shadow-casting alignments.

activities.title: Sequence, match and distinguish check
feedback: Correct ordering with reasons tied to orbital position shows the mechanism; ordering by rote alone should be revisited with the linked views.

If you call a crescent a 'partial eclipse', recall that the dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side seen at an angle (the bright sliver is part of its sunlit half), while an eclipse is a real shadow cast during a rare line-up.
If you expect a monthly eclipse, recall the tilted orbit usually carries the Moon just above or below the alignment, so the shadow misses.
activities.rationale: Recognition and matching tasks assess whether learners can apply the model but do not by themselves build the geometric intuition, so they work best after the hands-on and interactive work. Adding a short reasoning requirement surfaces residual misconceptions.
learnerActions: Put the eight phases in correct order from new Moon through full and back.
Match each top-down orbital position to the phase seen from Earth.
Given a described or drawn alignment, decide whether it is a solar eclipse (Moon between Sun and Earth) or a lunar eclipse (Earth between Sun and Moon).
In reasoning, explain why a crescent is NOT a partial eclipse, and why an eclipse does not happen every month.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to sequence phases, pair positions to views, and separate solar from lunar eclipses demonstrates the outcome of the geometric model; the reasoning items check whether the mechanism, not just the labels, is held.

constraints: Teach phases before eclipses, and keep them explicitly distinct: phases are a monthly consequence of viewing geometry; eclipses are rare alignments where a shadow actually falls, rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's.
Maintain the two-viewpoint discipline: present the God's-eye orbit view (Moon always half-lit) and the Earth-based sky view together and keep translating between them.

At full Moon, do not teach that Earth's shadow 'points away' from the Moon: the full Moon sits near the anti-solar point where Earth's umbra points, and it is usually not eclipsed only because the Moon's orbit is tilted. Use the crescent as the clean case where Earth's shadow is genuinely far from the Moon.

The sequence/matching/distinguish check tests the outcome but does not build spatial intuition on its own; place it after modelling. A static phase wheel is a reference and consolidation aid, not a substitute for seeing the phase morph or manipulating the geometry.

Approximate the phase cycle (new Moon to new Moon, the synodic month) as about 29.5 days; the Moon's orbit measured against the stars (the sidereal month) is about 27.3 days. The legacy '~28-day cycle' is only a rough approximation, and these figures should not all be presented as exactly correct.

The ball-and-lamp model needs a genuinely darkened room and a single bright source to read the lit fraction clearly; hold the ball slightly above head height so the learner's own head does not repeatedly block the lamp.
Avoid the 'dark side of the Moon' framing: the far side is not permanently dark, and the Moon is present in the daytime sky too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The legacy source for the Earth's-shadow misconception (Baxter / IOP-SPARK) is marked unverified in the row; treat the misconception's prevalence claim as reported, not independently confirmed here.

The orbital period is cited inconsistently in the source: the pedagogy states ~29.5 days while the assessment and descriptor state ~28 days. Activities use ~29.5 days and flag the discrepancy; a reviewer should settle on one figure (the synodic month is about 29.5 days).

The original recommendation and assessment describe Earth's shadow at full Moon as 'stretching off in the opposite direction', which is geometrically imprecise: a full Moon lies near the anti-solar point where Earth's umbra actually points, and it is usually not eclipsed because of the ~5 degree orbital tilt. Corrected in the activities and constraints; the crescent is used as the clean 'shadow is far away' demonstration.

The source's claim that linking the two views causes the Earth's-shadow misconception to 'collapse' and that an in-role conversation 'cannot deliver the aha' are catalog preference assertions; softened here to narrowly scoped affordances (manipulable linked views let learners test the shadow idea; a 3D model offers a different spatial experience). No comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.
The assessment field references a reteach prerequisite id for the phase-eclipse conflation; routing/prerequisite logic was not altered and is outside this learning-guidance rewrite.

assess.poeTask: In a darkened room use a single bright lamp as the Sun and give the child a ball on a stick as the Moon, with their own head as the Earth. Ask them to PREDICT with a reason: as you slowly turn the ball around your head, will it go through crescent → half → full, and what makes the dark part? Many predict their own head's (Earth's) shadow falls on the ball. Have them commit, then turn: the lit portion they see grows and shrinks purely with the angle to the lamp, and at 'full' their head's shadow misses the ball entirely. The pre-turn reason is diagnostic — predicting 'my shadow makes the dark part' is the Earth's-shadow misconception.
probeDeeper: If the phases were the Earth's shadow, how often would they happen — and could we ever see a full Moon?
How much of the Moon is lit by the Sun at any moment? So why don't we always see a full Moon?
What is actually different between a crescent Moon and a lunar eclipse?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon; phases are how much of that lit half we can SEE from Earth as the Moon orbits us — set by the changing angle between Sun, Earth and Moon. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not the Earth's shadow. The Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which is rare.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the phases are the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon' (the dominant Moon-phase misconception)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Couple an orbit-view with a sky-view and park at full Moon: the Earth's shadow points AWAY into space; the dark part is the Moon's own unlit side seen at an angle.
errorPatterns.distractor: The dark part is the Earth's shadow cast onto the Moon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes the dark part of the Moon to the Earth's shadow

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Moon makes its own light and gets covered up / dims itself' (Moon as light source; blocking)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight and half is always lit; phases are about our viewing angle, not the Moon changing its own light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: talks about the Moon's own light being blocked or the Moon dimming itself

errorPatterns.pattern: 'phases and eclipses are the same thing' (phase–eclipse conflation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Phases happen monthly (viewing angle); eclipses are rare alignments where a shadow really is cast, rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's.
errorPatterns.distractor: A crescent Moon is a partial eclipse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls a crescent a 'partial eclipse,' or says an eclipse should happen every month

responseLevels.gap: Attributes phases to the Earth's shadow, or thinks the Moon makes and loses its own light.
responseLevels.full: Explains phases as the changing amount of the always-half-lit Moon visible from Earth as it orbits, explicitly rejects the Earth's-shadow account (the shadow points away at full Moon), sequences the ~28-day cycle, and distinguishes solar from lunar eclipse; transfers.
responseLevels.partial: Knows phases come from the Sun–Earth–Moon arrangement and reflected light but still can't rule out the shadow, or conflates phases with eclipses.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Many people think the dark curved part of a crescent Moon is the Earth's shadow falling on it. What actually makes the Moon look like a crescent, a half, or full? … Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both the shadow account and the geometry account 'explain' a crescent, so tier one is silent — the reasoning tier separates them. A child citing the Earth's shadow reveals the dominant misconception; one citing the changing viewing angle of the always-half-lit Moon has the mechanism. If shadow were the cause, a 'phase' would appear whenever Earth's shadow fell, and a full Moon could never happen.
